slides.title: MLE and MAP are *one term apart*.
slides.sub: That term is everything you believed before the data arrived.

slides.quote: Three heads in three flips, and maximum likelihood says the coin is always heads.
slides.text: It is not wrong. It is answering exactly what you asked -- which value makes this data most probable -- with nothing else to go on.
slides.meta: field note · from the probability track

slides.text: Black is the likelihood: `p = 1` really does explain three heads best. Multiply it by the prior and the peak steps back off the wall.
slides.note: Each curve is scaled to its own peak, so the shapes are comparable.

bullets: **MLE** maximises `P(D | p)` -- how probable the data looks under one guess.
**MAP** maximises `P(p | D)` -- how probable that guess looks given the data.
**Bayes** links them: the posterior is the likelihood times the prior.
**The prior** `P(p)` is the only new factor. That is the entire difference.
**A flat prior** makes them identical -- MLE is MAP that believes nothing.
slides.note: The prior is a thumb on the scale. You get to say how heavy.

lines: # maximum likelihood: the data, and nothing else
# MAP with a Beta(a, b) prior: the same count,
# plus the a-1 heads and b-1 tails you assumed
# a = b = 1 is flat, and p_map == p_mle again
slides.note: Beta(2,2) is you admitting you have seen a coin before.

slides.text: Same coin, every flip a head. MLE is pinned at 1.00 from the first flip. MAP starts at 0.80 and closes the gap as the count climbs -- by forty flips the prior is worth 0.02.
slides.note: `(n + 1) / (n + 2)` when a = b = 2 -- two imagined flips, diluted.

slides.quote: MAP still hands you one number. The distribution it came from had a shape, and the mode is _not_ the mean unless that shape is kind.
slides.text: It is also not invariant: reparameterise and the mode moves, because the prior density moves with it. Maximum likelihood does not have that problem.
Linear algebra, calculus and probability from the axioms up -- one log at a time, in public.

caption:
Three heads in three flips and maximum likelihood will tell you the coin is always heads. That is not a bug, it is the whole design.

MLE maximises P(D | p). MAP maximises P(p | D). Bayes says the second is the first times your prior, so the only difference between them is one factor -- what you believed before the data arrived.

Slide 3 is the whole post in one picture: likelihood, prior and posterior on the same axis, and the peak visibly stepping back off the wall. With a Beta(2,2) prior those three flips give 0.80 instead of 1.00.

Slide 6 is the part nobody mentions -- keep flipping and the prior fades. By forty heads it is worth 0.02, and MAP has quietly become MLE again.

The catch: MAP is still one number out of a whole distribution, and it moves if you reparameterise. Maximum likelihood does not.
